African penguin deaths investigated

By: Annalise Lubbe | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In a freak event 63 African penguins died after being attacked by a swarm of Cape Honeybees at their Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town - a blow to the species already in trouble.

Unique Selling Point:
More than 60 endangered African penguins were killed by a swarm of Cape honey bees, in what conservationists described as an unusual occurrence. The 63 birds were found dead inside the Boulders Beach African penguin colony in Simon’s Town according to the South African National Parks (SANParks). The penguins died sometime between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning in September. A post-mortems revealed that all the penguins had multiple bee stings and many dead bees were found at the site where the birds had died.

Samples of the penguins were still being tested for other “toxicity possibilities and diseases'' to rule out other potential causes. The deaths come as a blow to conservation efforts to conserve the endangered species, which the Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) records as having a ‘declining’ population. African penguins have lost around half their population since the late 1970’s.


Summary:
Since the turn of the 20th century the world has lost 99% of the African penguin population. Today there are only 20 000 birds left in South Africa with roughly 2000 of these birds nesting in Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town. Sadly commercial fishing, oil spills and depleted prey populations have been the cause of their rapid decline and scientists predict they could be “functionally extinct” by 2035.

The penguins at Boulders Beach are a major attraction for tourists. Up to 60 000 visitors flock to see the birds in their natural habitat in a nature reserve. Co-existing with the penguins are the Cape honey bees who are only found in the Fynbos belt in the southern and western Cape.

The freak accident where 63 penguins were killed in a short period of time has been described as unusual by scientists as this is the first time that the African Penguins have been attacked by such a large swarm of Cape honeybees and stung multiple times. The bee stings were found around their eyes and on their flippers where there are no feathers to protect them. Some penguins were stung more than 20 times which would kill a bird of that size.


Further information:
The morning after SANParks staff found the dead penguins on the beach there were many speculations. At first they suspected a predator (Caracel) had moved into the colony but there were no physical signs of injury, then they worried it was some kind of avian flu but the penguins had not shown any typical signs. Then they went back to the site and found dead bees in the sight where the dead penguins were found. Post mortems on carcasses of the birds then confirmed that the culprit was the Cape honey bee.

Usually a larger colony would be able to withstand such an attack but this particular species is considered endangered and losing several dozen will prove a blow. Authorities are now searching for the hive to find out what may have triggered the swarm. SANCCOB says it's just bad luck for the penguins and they don’t expect this to happen more often as the bees are normally not a threat for the penguins. But only time will tell.

Speculations are that a nest or hive in the area was disturbed by an intruder or noise factor which caused the bees to fly in direction where unfortunately the penguins became the victims as they were in their direct flight path. There are still more tests to be done as no definitive answers have yet been found.

The long-term effect on what transpired has scientists worried as it is more than just the loss of 63 birds. Penguins mate for life and with one adult bird gone, who will help to raise the new-born chicks? Will they end up in rehabilitation as they are too weak to fend for themselves and how long will it take before a new partner is found and the breeding can start again. These are all questions that need answers.

Our interviews:
Alison Kock, a marine biologist from South African National Parks (SANParks) who formed part of the team of specialists investigating the case.
Dr. Katta Ludynia, research Manager at SANCCOB who formed part of the team at the rehabilitation centre where post mortems were performed and test done.
Jenny Cullinan, bee expert and conservationist who have conducted research on the Cape honey bee for five years and have made an in depth study of their behavioural patterns and habits.

Treatment
The story will be told in a ‘who-dunnit’ style where suspense builds up by asking questions and leaving the viewer with a sense of apprehension. Low point of view camera angles will be used on a mini camera to create the illusion of a bee flying through the Fynbos. Digital sound effects will create an almost digital sound where maps will be used to indicate territory and locations. Aerial views will be intercut with very low angle shots mixing between certain colours to add to the flight patterns and habits of the two different species.

There will be a fair amount of re-enactment and setting up visuals to tell the story as we did not catch the event as it unfolded. There are a number of images and a video clip available as proof of what happened but the rest will have to be created.

The links will be done as a ‘who-dunnit’ style with the presenter looking at footprints of who is the culprit and asking questions about the ‘scene of the crime’, leaving the viewer in suspense till the end.

Presenter flight to CT, accommodation for one night

Script:


Final Script: Penguin deaths investigated
Duration: 8 Minutes
Date: 7 September 2021

V/O On the shores of Simon’s Town at the southern tip of the Western Cape lies Boulders Beach: the home of the African Penguin. This is a favourite tourist spot for visitors to watch the penguins as they go about their business in the safety of the Table Mountain National Park.

LINK: A seaside town and a peaceful scene of sun and sand and visitors enjoying the site of penguins in their colony. It sounds idyllic but in September this scene changed dramatically in a matter of hours.

Dr Alison Kock: Marine Biologist: SANParks - Early on Friday morning I got a call from one of the staff members that they found a group of dead penguins on the beach not far away from here.

Claire Mawisa: What was your initial thought when you did get on site, when you did see the dead penguins?

Dr Alison Kock: It was a big shock to us. These penguins are endangered so losing penguins like that is of concern to us. What we found was quite a large number of dead penguins in a very localised area of the colony and we had no idea at the time what had happened. We immediately started looking around the colony to check on the rest of the birds.

Up sound

V/O If a predator were on the prowl, penguins would raise an alarm if threatened. It’s thought the wooden fence protects them from predators …..but can it keep smaller threats out? SANParks rangers patrol regular rounds to check on the birds.

LINK: It was a Thursday afternoon and the rangers had done their last round patrolling the beaches and checking that the penguins were safe and settled in for the night.

V/O By Friday morning the scene had changed dramatically. Dozens of birds were found on a small patch of the beach, some washed out by the tide and others covered with windblown sand.

LINK: When experts look for clues they start with evidence found at the scene of the crime: footprints, blood on rocks or any other clues that will help them with their investigation but what they found surprised everyone.

Dr Alison Kock: At the start we were really unsure of what it could be but we suspected possibly some sort of pollution event, possibly a poisoning event, possibly an illness that was very rapid because none of the birds had any external physical injuries. They looked in good physical condition except that they were dead. So it was really a mystery to us.

V/O With no visible attack marks, predators were ruled out. There were no indications of the usual threats like oil spills or red tide. The search continued: 63 dead mpenguins were found - all adults in the prime of their lives. More experts were brought in.

Dr Katta Ludynia - Research Manager SANCCOB: So early in the morning I got a phone call from the City of CT that we work very closely with that one of the SANParks staff had actually seen some dead penguins on the beach and they weren’t quite sure of what had happened.

V/O With no visible clues, further investigation involved post mortems and testing the birds for toxins or possible diseases. SANCCOB is the largest seabird hospital in southern Africa treating over 1000 African penguins every year: from oil spills to injured birds here they stand a chance to survive and be put back in the wild. The latest casualties consituted a freak event - a first of this magnitude.

LINK: The dead penguins were brought here to SANCCOB so that post mortems could be performed so that they could determine the cause of death.

Dr. Katta Ludynia: So we have an issue currently with avian influenza so that was one of the thoughts. It was very strange as it was very localised. So if it was avian influenza or algal bloom or something we would have expected it to have affected the entire colony.

V/O Blood samples testing for avian influenza and other diseases came back - negative! Meanwhile the post mortems continued.

Dr. Katta Ludynia: So they look at the condition of the birds and then they start opening them up to see if there are any changes in the organs, anything that can indicate why these birds died. They found slight changes in the organs; internal bleeding which can be caused by a lot of different things.

V/O After working through the night on several carcasses there was a breakthrough! The evidence was found around the soft part of the eyes. Beestings!

Dr Alison Kock: While we were working in the colony the vets at SANCCOB were doing the post mortems and we were in constant communication with them. And it was only late in the evening that the vet from SANCCOB let me know that he’d found multiple bee stings around the eyes of one of the penguins.

Dr Katta Ludynia: Our researcher that was doing the post mortems he realised that in that little skin part that they have around their eyes he could see like kind of little dots and when he actually started looking at it in more detail he could pull out the bee stings. And he realised that every bird had like over 20 stings just around and some of them like on the inside of the flippers.

LINK: They went back to the site and found their clue: dead bees where the penguins were killed.

V/O Jenny Cullinan, a wild bee expert was called in to help identify the culprits - she examined the evidence.

Clair Mawisa: And what did you find when you got there?

Jenny Cullinan: Wild bee expert - They had little jars of dead bees in them and they wanted me to identify if they were the Cape honeybee and they had their stings and they showed me all the photographs and also where the penguins had been and the blood all over the rocks. So it was quite a distressing thing to see.

V/O The marks on the rocks that looked like blood, was red excrement from internal bleeding as the bee venom affected organs.

Clair: So when you got there what were your initial thoughts?

Jenny Cullinan: This kind of attack from honeybees can only happen when their home is threatened. So wherever they had come from they have had to have somebody damaging their home so they had to leave with their queen. And the way in which bees protect themselves and their colony would be to sting. So if they sting something they lose their life so it is a big loss to the penguins and a big loss to the colony that was on the move.

Claire Mawisa: How many bees were they talking about?

Jenny Cullinan: There were lots of dead bees so every time the penguins were stung those bees would have died so there were probably hundreds of dead bees.

V/O The Cape honeybee is unique to South Africa and found only in the Fynbos belt of the southern and western Cape. Simon’s Town lies in the buffer zone in the Table Mountain National Park where Cullinan had been studying the wild bees and their behavioural patterns for over 8 years.

LINK: This is the nest of the cape honeybee and you can see they live in peace and harmony undisturbed and happy but should i put my hand in there and disturb them they would defend their nest and attack me by stinging.

Claire Mawisa: Are bees a threat to our penguins?

Jenny Cullinan: The threat comes in when we disturb them, only when their homes are threatened and damaged does this happen. This is not what bees do: they don’t go out killing things without a reason.

V/O The loss of the bees is as important as the loss of the birds. Both species face an uncertain future. Bees, under threat globally from the use of insecticide and climate change, and insect populations declining rapidly. At the turn of the 20th century the world lost 99% of the African penguin population. Today there are only 20 000 birds left in South Africa with roughly 2000 nesting in the Boulders Beach colony.

Dr Alison Kock: The penguin and the bees are both very important components to the ecosystem here and they coexist on a daily basis. The main problems facing penguins is a lack of food. And we really need to make sure that the population is healthy enough to withstand these kinds of rare and unusual events in the colony.

Promo 1: 22 seconds
V/O In a freak event 63 endangered African penguins died in a matter of hours after being stung by a swarm of bees at their Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town.
Jenny Cullinan: This kind of attack from honeybees can only happen when their home is threatened.

Promo 2: 22 seconds
Dr Alison Kock - Early on Friday morning I got a call from one of the staff members that they found a group of dead penguins on the beach not far away from here.
V/O Dozens of endangered penguins were found dead on a popular beach in Simon’s Town. No visible clues were left to their cause of death until scientists found the culprit. Beestings!

Promo 3: 11 seconds
V/O In a freak event 63 African penguins were stung to death after being attacked by a swarm of Cape honeybees in their Simon’s Town colony - a blow to the species already in trouble.

Dr Katta Ludynia: Our researcher that was doing the post mortems he realised that in that little skin part that they have around their eyes he could see like kind of little dots and when he actually started looking at it in more detail he could pull out the bee stings. And he realised that every bird had like over 20 stings just around and some of them like on the inside of the flippers. LINK: They went back to the site and found their clue: dead bees where the penguins were killed. V/O Jenny Cullinan, a wild bee expert was called in to help identify the culprits - she examined the evidence. Clair Mawisa: And what did you find when you got there? Jenny Cullinan: Wild bee expert - They had little jars of dead bees in them and they wanted me to identify if they were the Cape honeybee and they had their stings and they showed me all the photographs and also where the penguins had been and the blood all over the rocks. So it was quite a distressing thing to see. V/O The marks on the rocks that looked like blood, was red excrement from internal bleeding as the bee venom affected organs. Clair: So when you got there what were your initial thoughts? Jenny Cullinan: This kind of attack from honeybees can only happen when their home is threatened. So wherever they had come from they have had to have somebody damaging their home so they had to leave with their queen. And the way in which bees protect themselves and their colony would be to sting. So if they sting something they lose their life so it is a big loss to the penguins and a big loss to the colony that was on the move. Claire Mawisa: How many bees were they talking about? Jenny Cullinan: There were lots of dead bees so every time the penguins were stung those bees would have died so there were probably hundreds of dead bees. V/O The Cape honeybee is unique to South Africa and found only in the Fynbos belt of the southern and western Cape. Simon’s Town lies in the buffer zone in the Table Mountain National Park where Cullinan had been studying the wild bees and their behavioural patterns for over 8 years. LINK: This is the nest of the cape honeybee and you can see they live in peace and harmony undisturbed and happy but should i put my hand in there and disturb them they would defend their nest and attack me by stinging. Claire Mawisa: Are bees a threat to our penguins? Jenny Cullinan: The threat comes in when we disturb them, only when their homes are threatened and damaged does this happen. This is not what bees do: they don’t go out killing things without a reason. V/O The loss of the bees is as important as the loss of the birds. Both species face an uncertain future. Bees, under threat globally from the use of insecticide and climate change, and insect populations declining rapidly. At the turn of the 20th century the world lost 99% of the African penguin population. Today there are only 20 000 birds left in South Africa with roughly 2000 nesting in the Boulders Beach colony. Dr Alison Kock: The penguin and the bees are both very important components to the ecosystem here and they coexist on a daily basis. The main problems facing penguins is a lack of food. And we really need to make sure that the population is healthy enough to withstand these kinds of rare and unusual events in the colony. ______________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1: 22 seconds V/O In a freak event 63 endangered African penguins died in a matter of hours after being stung by a swarm of bees at their Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town. Jenny Cullinan: This kind of attack from honeybees can only happen when their home is threatened. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): In a freak event 63 African penguins died after being attacked by a swarm of Cape Honeybees at their Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town - a blow to the species already in trouble.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: More than 60 endangered African penguins were killed by a swarm of Cape honey bees, in what conservationists described as an unusual occurrence. The 63 birds were found dead inside the Boulders Beach African penguin colony in Simon’s Town according to the South African National Parks (SANParks). The penguins died sometime between Thursday afternoon and Friday morning in September. A post-mortems revealed that all the penguins had multiple bee stings and many dead bees were found at the site where the birds had died. Samples of the penguins were still being tested for other “toxicity possibilities and diseases'' to rule out other potential causes. The deaths come as a blow to conservation efforts to conserve the endangered species, which the Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) records as having a ‘declining’ population. African penguins have lost around half their population since the late 1970’s.
metadata.Summary: Since the turn of the 20th century the world has lost 99% of the African penguin population. Today there are only 20 000 birds left in South Africa with roughly 2000 of these birds nesting in Boulders Beach colony in Simon’s Town. Sadly commercial fishing, oil spills and depleted prey populations have been the cause of their rapid decline and scientists predict they could be “functionally extinct” by 2035. The penguins at Boulders Beach are a major attraction for tourists. Up to 60 000 visitors flock to see the birds in their natural habitat in a nature reserve. Co-existing with the penguins are the Cape honey bees who are only found in the Fynbos belt in the southern and western Cape. The freak accident where 63 penguins were killed in a short period of time has been described as unusual by scientists as this is the first time that the African Penguins have been attacked by such a large swarm of Cape honeybees and stung multiple times. The bee stings were found around their eyes and on their flippers where there are no feathers to protect them. Some penguins were stung more than 20 times which would kill a bird of that size.
metadata.Further information: The morning after SANParks staff found the dead penguins on the beach there were many speculations. At first they suspected a predator (Caracel) had moved into the colony but there were no physical signs of injury, then they worried it was some kind of avian flu but the penguins had not shown any typical signs. Then they went back to the site and found dead bees in the sight where the dead penguins were found. Post mortems on carcasses of the birds then confirmed that the culprit was the Cape honey bee. Usually a larger colony would be able to withstand such an attack but this particular species is considered endangered and losing several dozen will prove a blow. Authorities are now searching for the hive to find out what may have triggered the swarm. SANCCOB says it's just bad luck for the penguins and they don’t expect this to happen more often as the bees are normally not a threat for the penguins. But only time will tell. Speculations are that a nest or hive in the area was disturbed by an intruder or noise factor which caused the bees to fly in direction where unfortunately the penguins became the victims as they were in their direct flight path. There are still more tests to be done as no definitive answers have yet been found. The long-term effect on what transpired has scientists worried as it is more than just the loss of 63 birds. Penguins mate for life and with one adult bird gone, who will help to raise the new-born chicks? Will they end up in rehabilitation as they are too weak to fend for themselves and how long will it take before a new partner is found and the breeding can start again. These are all questions that need answers. Our interviews: Alison Kock, a marine biologist from South African National Parks (SANParks) who formed part of the team of specialists investigating the case. Dr. Katta Ludynia, research Manager at SANCCOB who formed part of the team at the rehabilitation centre where post mortems were performed and test done. Jenny Cullinan, bee expert and conservationist who have conducted research on the Cape honey bee for five years and have made an in depth study of their behavioural patterns and habits. Treatment The story will be told in a ‘who-dunnit’ style where suspense builds up by asking questions and leaving the viewer with a sense of apprehension. Low point of view camera angles will be used on a mini camera to create the illusion of a bee flying through the Fynbos. Digital sound effects will create an almost digital sound where maps will be used to indicate territory and locations. Aerial views will be intercut with very low angle shots mixing between certain colours to add to the flight patterns and habits of the two different species. There will be a fair amount of re-enactment and setting up visuals to tell the story as we did not catch the event as it unfolded. There are a number of images and a video clip available as proof of what happened but the rest will have to be created. The links will be done as a ‘who-dunnit’ style with the presenter looking at footprints of who is the culprit and asking questions about the ‘scene of the crime’, leaving the viewer in suspense till the end.
